data.title: Tejon Ranch Earnings Call Shows Growth and Challenges
data.description:
Tejon Ranch ((TRC)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Tejon Ranch delivered a broadly positive third quarter, with gains in revenue, net income, adjusted EBITDA, mineral resources, occupancy and multifamily activity. Management nevertheless cautioned that unusual timing items, higher net debt, cash-consuming operations and a demanding cost structure mean the transformation is still underway.

Revenue and Earnings Improve

Third-quarter revenue, net income and adjusted EBITDA all exceeded last year’s levels, while year-to-date results were comparable. Net income attributable to common stockholders rose to $3.3 million, or $0.12 per share, from $1.7 million, or $0.06 per share, a year earlier.

Adjusted EBITDA Nearly Doubles

Adjusted EBITDA nearly doubled to $10.4 million from $5.3 million, reflecting stronger performance across much of the operating portfolio. Trailing-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA also climbed about 44% to $35 million from $24.3 million.

Mineral Resources Lead Operating Growth

Mineral Resources revenue increased 25%, while operating income rose nearly 58%, making the segment a major contributor to the quarter’s improvement. National Cement also exercised a 20-year lease extension, continuing a longstanding relationship and supporting the property’s long-term value.

Commercial Portfolio Remains Well Occupied

Tejon Ranch’s commercial and industrial assets maintained high occupancy, with industrial properties fully leased and commercial occupancy at 95%. The results point to continued demand for the company’s strategically located real estate portfolio.

Terra Vista Leasing Gains Momentum

Leasing progress at Terra Vista helped lift multifamily revenue to $924,000 from $181,000 last year. The increase highlights the growing contribution from the apartment business, although construction spending on the project remains an important use of cash.

Lower Corporate Costs and Better Farming Results

Corporate expenses, including share-based compensation adjustments, fell 40% during the quarter and 22% year to date after excluding prior-year non-recurring costs. Adjusted farming EBITDA before fixed water obligations increased to $2.6 million from $425,000, aided by stronger agricultural results.

Commerce Center Construction Advances

Commerce Center Building 1B, being developed with Dedeaux Properties, remains under construction and is progressing toward completion early next year. Management described the joint venture as a capital-efficient model that uses third-party equity and targets strong returns, a structure it hopes to repeat.

Hard Rock Expansion Supports Development Plans

The Tejon Indian Tribe and Hard Rock International broke ground on the next phase of Hard Rock Casino Tejon, including a 406-room hotel and entertainment venue. Management expects the investment to broaden the customer base and create a wider positive impact across the Commerce Center.

Water Sales and Agricultural Timing Affect Results

Tejon Ranch sold a substantial portion of its water before the market changed sharply after a strong El Niño winter, while management said it remains positioned to respond when future demand allows. An early wine-grape harvest shifted sales into the third quarter, and warm spring weather affected almond sizing, with the effect on total yield to be reported at year-end.

Residential Entitlements Move Forward

Kern County approved an amendment to the Grapevine Specific Plan, updating the land-use mix and phasing and moving the project closer to mapping and its first phase reaching the market. At Centennial, the company is processing an updated application before reviews by the Regional Planning Commission and Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors.

Capital Search Continues for Tejon Mountain Village

The fully entitled Tejon Mountain Village remains in the capitalization process as Tejon Ranch seeks investment partners with assistance from outside investment banking resources. The effort is part of management’s broader attempt to turn land holdings into recurring income and improve capital efficiency.

Liquidity Provides Financial Flexibility

The company ended September with approximately $74.4 million of liquidity, including $8.8 million in cash and marketable securities and $65.6 million available under its revolving credit facility. Total debt was $94.4 million, equal to about 16% of total capitalization, although management emphasized that interest expense remains significant.

Operating Cash Flow Improves

Tejon Ranch generated more than $7 million in operating cash this year, compared with about $4 million consumed in the prior year, an improvement of roughly $11 million. Excluding Terra Vista apartment construction, cash use was approximately $14 million lower than a year ago.

One-Time Items Lifted Quarterly Comparisons

Management said the earnings improvement included timing and non-recurring effects, including a second-quarter land-sale contribution from the Dedeaux industrial joint venture, $3.9 million of crop insurance proceeds and $2.6 million of bonus price adjustments tied to last year’s pistachio crop. These items make the quarter stronger but less representative of underlying recurring performance.

Debt and Cost Structure Remain Concerns

Net debt increased $16 million year to date, even though actual borrowings rose only $500,000, with debt reductions expected to follow cash-generating activities. Management acknowledged that some businesses generate cash while others, along with corporate overhead, consume it, and agreed that further cost reductions are needed.

Transformation Requires Capital Discipline

Management is seeking to build a more effective land-company model around Tejon Ranch’s location between Northern and Southern California and the Commerce Center’s industrial, retail, multifamily and travel-center network. It also acknowledged that revenue must rise while controllable costs and discretionary capital spending fall, helping convert assets into durable cash flow.

Share Price Valuation Remains a Frustration

Management said the shares trade below its view of the intrinsic value of the company’s assets, a concern shared by investors. Narrowing that gap will require disciplined capital deployment, stronger recurring cash flow, lower costs and better conversion of land assets into operating returns.

Forward-Looking Guidance

Building 1B remains on track for completion early next year, while Grapevine moves toward mapping and its first phase reaching the market. Centennial is expected to undergo county reviews in the coming months, and the company will continue seeking capital partners for Tejon Mountain Village while working to reduce debt, costs and discretionary capital spending, increase revenue and report fourth-quarter results early next year.

Overall, Tejon Ranch posted meaningful operating improvements, led by higher EBITDA, mineral resources performance, occupancy and multifamily revenue. The gains were tempered by one-time items, rising net debt and cash-flow challenges, leaving investors focused on whether management can turn development assets into recurring income while maintaining disciplined spending.
